messages.author: 55fd48251ccdf5a6
messages.subject: multiple indexing in matrices
parts:
Hi all,

 

I have a data matrix with missing and observed values. Missing values do not really have a specific pattern and thus I want to estimate them in the posterior.

I tried the multiple indexing in the stan manual (in 25.5) in order to mix missing values and observed ones in the same matrix (as transformed parameter) but I keep getting a type mismatch error.

I  also tried Ben’s code in the reply in this thread (which is the same as in the manual) : https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/kpkKWTvoEks

 

The code is the following:

transformed data { // you could also pass these in as data
  int<lower=1,upper=3> row_mark[7];
  int<lower=1,upper=3> col_mark[7];
  row_mark[1] <- 1; col_mark[1] <- 1;
  row_mark[2] <- 2; col_mark[2] <- 1;
  row_mark[3] <- 3; col_mark[3] <- 1;
  row_mark[4] <- 2; col_mark[4] <- 2;
  row_mark[5] <- 3; col_mark[5] <- 2;
  row_mark[6] <- 2; col_mark[6] <- 3;
  row_mark[7] <- 3; col_mark[7] <- 3;
}
parameters {
  vector[7] Bvec;
}
model {
  matrix[3,3] B;
  B[row_mark,col_mark] <- Bvec;


  B[1,2] <- 0;
  B[1,3] <- 0;
}

 

However, I keep getting the following error in stan:

 

SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
 
base type mismatch in assignment; variable name=B, type=matrix; right-hand side type=vector
Illegal statement beginning with non-void expression parsed as
  B[row_mark, col_mark]
Not a legal assignment, sampling, or function statement.  Note that
  * Assignment statements only allow variables (with optional indexes) on the left;
    if you see an outer function logical_lt (<) with negated (-) second argument,
    it indicates an assignment statement A <- B with illegal left
    side A parsed as expression (A < (-B)).
  * Sampling statements allow arbitrary value-denoting expressions on the left.
  * Functions used as statements must be declared to have void returns
 
 
ERROR at line 17
 
 15:    model {
 16:    matrix[3,3] B;
 17:    B[row_mark,col_mark] = Bvec;
        ^
 18:    B[1,2] = 0;
 
PARSER EXPECTED: "}"
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  : 
  failed to parse Stan model 'breg' due to the above error.

 

The parser seems to identify B[row_mark,col_mark]  as a matrix although it is a vector. I am wondering if I missed something as I am new to stan and used to jags and winbugs syntax.

 

Many thanks in advance,

 

Takoua Jendoubi

PhD student

School of Public Health & Department of Surgery and Cancer

Main address :

Imperial College London | Room 171 | St Mary’s Campus | Norfolk Place | London | W2 1PG |

I think you're right. I had to change the definition of Bvec to either a matrix[7, 1] or a matrix[1, 7] to get this to compile happily, but the manual clearly shows Bvec as a vector. This definitely seems like a bug with either Stan or the manual. Head over to the Github and make an issue: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues

This mailing list is moving to http://discourse.mc-stan.org/ by the way. Might get quicker feedback if you make new issues over there.

Cheers
Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] multiple indexing in matrices
parts:
Your error messages will make more sense if you replace the <- with =.
It falls back to trying to interpret < as less-than and - as negation in
some cases.

What's happening is that B[row_mark, col_mark] is a scalar and you're trying
to assigna vector to it.

If you want to mix in values, use the long form.

data {
int I;
int J;
int N_obs;
int ii_obs[N_obs];
int jj_obs[N_obs];
real y_obs[N_obs]
int N_un;
int ii_un[N_un];
int jj_un[N_un];

parameters {
real y_un[N_un];

transformed parameters {
matrix[I, J] y;
for (n in 1:N_obs)
y[ii_obs[n], jj_obs[n]] = y_obs[n];
for (n in 1:_N_un)
y[ii_un[n], jj_un[n]] = y_un[n];

- Bob

Many thanks.

I tried to print B[row_mark, col_mark] which was a duplicated matrix of B according to the indexes in row_mark and col_mark. i.e if B is a 3X3, B[row_mark, col_mark] is a 7X7 matrix. replacing Bvec to either a matrix[7, 1] or a matrix[1, 7] removes the mismatch error. However the sampler never succeeds to find plausible initialization values.
Only the long form that Bob recommended worked.

parts:
Multi-indexing matrices works just like in R. The key to understanding it is that
if you have this:

matrix[M, N] a;

int<lower=1, upper=M> rs[I];
int<lower=1, upper=N> cs[J];

then the way a[rs, cs] is defined produces an I x J matrix
whose entries are defined as

a[rs, cs][i, j] = a[rs[i], cs[j]]

- Bob
